figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: The session state machine that every session runs. Solid edges are the checked transition table; a transition not in the table raises an error instead of being taken. Two escapes bypass the table from any state: an unhandled fault ends the session in ERROR, and a cancellation from outside the loop ends it in STOPPED. STOPPED is a controlled stop at a limit or a refusal, with the reason recorded (Table 16), not a fault. Each end state returns to IDLE only when a new turn starts.
figures.headline: Any state transition outside the checked table raises an error, and limit stops end a session in a controlled STOPPED state.
citing_sentences: A transition that is not in the table of legal transitions raises an error instead of being taken (Figure 13).

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Two controllers over one session runtime. The Team controller opens a session for every declared role, each with its own token allowance; the model decides whether to hand work on with message_agent, and a message along an undeclared edge is refused and recorded. The Workflow controller is a Python script that fixes the order of work and opens one session per step; a single-agent run is one session with no controller above it. All sessions run the same code, which checks every limit before a model call, acts in the role’s workspace, and writes to one ordered event stream per run (Appendix C.6).
figures.headline: Team and Workflow controllers both run sessions on one runtime, and messages along undeclared edges are refused and recorded.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Figure 14 (Appendix C.1), this design separates the high-level orchestration of agent interactions from the low-level mechanics of model execution.
For resource control, Figure 14 shows how the runtime enforces an identical per-role token ceiling via pre-call admission within the session state machine.
Above the loop, a controller decides which sessions exist, when each one starts, and how their outputs travel (Figure 14).

abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration and controlled causal evaluation.

sections.body: The paper argues that configured multi-agent coding teams often do not collaborate as declared, so benchmark gains cannot be attributed to the organization. It introduces OpenCollab, which provides organization design, a shared runtime and fine-grained event streams. It defines Adherence, the rate at which a declared organization is realized, and the complier average causal effect (CACE) for attribution. Changing any one of five dimensions (model, tool set, budget, context, topology) shifts Adherence from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. OpenCollab (Duo) reaches 68.91% on SWE-bench Pro, 83.15% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 65.49% on DeepSWE. An audit of ten frameworks finds none that guarantees controlled comparison or verifies behavioral delivery.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Configured multi-agent teams often fail to collaborate as declared, so benchmarks cannot show whether an organization helps.

sections.body: This section argues that configured teams often do not collaborate. In trajectory analysis, the lead agent frequently bypasses teammates or exhausts its token allowance before any handoff, and Adherence frequently falls below half. The authors call this the illusion of collaboration. Mandating delegation in prompts makes Adherence swing widely. Keeping only collaborating runs creates post-treatment selection bias that penalizes the multi-agent arm. The causes are decentralized budgets not gated across the team and prose logs that lack role-level attribution. Table 1 audits seven conditions for controlled evaluation, and OpenCollab is the only artifact with every condition checked.
sections.heading: 2 Motivation
sections.headline: Configured teams often collapse into single-agent loops, and prompt or log-filtering fixes introduce bias.

sections.body: The section describes a two-layer design in which every role runs the same ten-state session loop on a shared runtime. A team controller lets the model decide whether to delegate along declared topology edges. A workflow controller follows a Python script with a fixed call order. The authors report that reproducing a multi-agent pattern from edict, at ~24k lines of code, needs 239 lines. Controls are enforced at invocation: out-of-role tool calls, undeclared messages and token overruns are refused and recorded. A run is adherent only when every applicable one of six axes is judged adherent. The complier effect is the Pass@1 difference from Single divided by Adherence, valid under a mean exclusion restriction. The experiments do not report the cost metrics.
sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.headline: OpenCollab separates a shared runtime from controllers, gates limits before each call, and scores runs from event streams.

sections.body: Table 2 compares six harnesses with GPT-5.6-Luna on SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE. OpenCollab (Duo) has the highest Pass@1 on all three, at 68.91%, 83.15% and 65.49%. OpenCollab (Base) uses the fewest tokens and the lowest cost. Paired by task against Base, Duo solves 18.58% of DeepSWE tasks that Base fails and fails 8.85% that Base solves. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 the split of 10.11% and 6.74% is too close to separate. Duo spends more tokens because it runs two complete solving processes. Table 3 varies five dimensions from a Qwen3.8-Flash reference with 47.2% Adherence, and GPT-5.6-Luna reaches 97.2%. Table 4 shows an Open-card Pass@1 difference of +5.6 becoming +11.8 after dividing by Adherence, which the authors say does not by itself indicate a violation.
sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.headline: Duo scores highest on all three benchmarks, and single-dimension ablations move Adherence between 47.2% and 97.2%.

sections.body: The related work places multi-agent coding within organization theory. It surveys systems such as self-collaboration, multi-agent interaction frameworks and stateful graphs, which the authors say lower the engineering barrier but mix organizational design with execution. It reviews debate, voting and repeated sampling alongside reports of mixed or negative returns, including under equal token budgets. The authors attribute conflicting findings to comparisons that do not hold budgets, toolsets or harnesses constant. Work on interaction networks finds that designated coordinator roles often fail to form communication hubs. The authors state that existing frameworks treat execution as an unverified black box, which OpenCollab addresses with event streams and Adherence.
sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.headline: Prior studies report mixed returns from multi-agent systems, yet platforms rarely verify that the assigned organization ran.

sections.body: The conclusion states that existing frameworks entangle organizational design with execution mechanics. OpenCollab separates them on a shared substrate with identical runtime semantics. It tracks Adherence to verify that configured collaboration occurs. The authors report that agents collaborate very differently across configurations, so evaluations that do not verify collaboration cannot attribute their gains to it. They claim OpenCollab provides both programmability and a controlled runtime for causal attribution under explicit identification. The acknowledgments thank four contributors for early work.
sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.headline: OpenCollab decouples design from execution, so collaboration can be verified and its gains attributed under stated assumptions.

sections.body: The appendix treats the Wald ratio ITT divided by Adherence as the complier average causal effect under a mean exclusion restriction. Theorem A.1 decomposes ITT into Adherence times CACE plus one minus Adherence times the non-adherent contrast. Proposition A.2 gives the exact discrepancy and sensitivity bounds when that restriction fails. Paired records can estimate the non-adherent contrast, which the authors say provides evidence rather than proof of exclusion. The section lists reporting requirements and states that an unverifiable axis verdict counts as non-adherent. Section C.7 defines six adherence axes: participation, delegation, role boundary, budget sharing, information flow and context policy.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives identification theory for the complier average causal effect, a sensitivity analysis, paired diagnostics, reporting requirements and adherence axes.
